newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Distillate stock build seen in API data.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Distillate stock build seen in API data.

text.p: High refiner output amid mostly above average temperatures in the U.S. Northeast will have boosted distillate stocks once again in the American Petroleum Institute's (API) oil inventory data, traders said.
"Production remains hefty, but demand was relatively weak," said Sweeney Oil trader Jim Ritterbusch.

A Reuters survey said traders on average were expecting a minor build of 500,000 barrels for distillate stocks which are comprised of heating oil and diesel. The API data, expected Thursday evening, reflects the week ended December 20.
Distillate stock estimates ranged from a draw of 300,000 to up one million barrels after building 1.05 million barrels for the week ended December 13.
Crude stocks were seen rising about two million barrels due to higher imports, particulary from the North Sea, which has seen the Europe-to-U.S. Gulf Coast arbitrage open.
In fact, traders said three Wall Street firms and one U.K. producer are now offering Brent cargoes for the second half of January.
"We will see a higher level of crude imports" said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt.

Estimates for crude stocks ranged from up one million to up three million barrels. The transatlantic arbitrage had been closed due to a run-up in oil prices and contributed to a shortfall in crude stocks which are now down 21.1 million barrels from a year ago.

Imports were also seen boosting gasoline stocks. Estimates ranged from down 1.5 million to up 2.2 million barrels as traders were mixed on the level of domestic demand. But, all agreed that U.S. demand for European gasoline has been steady.

The estimate average for gasoline was a build of 600,000 barrels. Dealers said recent refiner turnarounds should moderate capacity utilization rates by about 0.25 percentage point from a high 93.5 percent seen in last week's data.
Distillate output was expected to remain near 3.6 million barrels as refiners replenished depleted heat stocks before the output focus switches to gasoline ahead of spring demand.

Indeed, Colonial Pipeline Co said last week that it extended its space allocations through January 1997 since there was more demand to ship distillate than its huge Houston-to-New York distillate line could handle.

Meanwhile, the key heating oil market of the northeastern United States did not see the frigid weather that was expected a week ago. A cold front that froze the Midwest did not hit the Northeast until last Saturday, dampening heating oil demand in the region, dealers said.
